{{Short description|British chemist (1922–1985)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2019}}
'''Victor Gold''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry|FRSC]]<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Albery | first1 = W. J. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1987.0010  | doi-access = free| title = Victor Gold. 29 June 1922-29 September 1985 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 33 | pages = 262–288| year = 1987 | jstor = 769953| s2cid = 73043269 }}</ref> (29 June 1922 – 29 September 1985) was a [[chemist]] who served on the faculty of [[King's College, London]].<ref>Carsten Reinhardt (2001), ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=d26SRPGBDgUC&dq=victor+gold+chemistry+Advances+in+Physical+Organic+Chemistry&pg=PA20 Chemical sciences in the 20th century]'', page 20. Wiley-VCH, {{ISBN|3-527-30271-9}}, {{ISBN|978-3-527-30271-0}}</ref>

Gold was born in [[Vienna]], the son of lawyer Oscar Gold and his first wife, the former Emmy Kopperl. He was raised primarily by his mother.<ref name="frs"/> Gold arrived in England, at [[Croydon Airport|Croydon aerodrome]],  in the spring of 1938, aged 15. His entry to the UK had been arranged by his uncle Max Gold (father of [[Thomas Gold]], FRS). He was sent, with a cousin, to [[Loughborough College]] to learn English and work in the engineering workshops (probably with [[Herbert Schofield]]).

By the autumn of 1939, Gold had gained a place at University College (transferred to King's and Bristol, because of the war) to study chemistry, but the following summer all Austrian and German aliens were interned, mostly in [[Douglas, Isle of Man]]. In the camp Gold met Hans Pelzer, one of the founders of [[Transition state theory#Potential energy surfaces|transition state theory]], who taught Victor some [[quantum mechanics]].

Gold was released from internment in December 1940, and joined [[University College London|UCL]], now in [[Aberystwyth]];<ref>{{cite web|title=UCL Aberystwyth Prospectus, 1942|website=Collecting: Knowledge in Motion|url=http://www.opendutch.org/kimotion/items/show/13|access-date=5 May 2020}}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Bristol was out of bounds for him. After a poor start he gained a first-class honours degree, largely thanks to the encouragement of [[Christopher Kelk Ingold|Sir Christopher Ingold]].
In 1944, Gold was appointed Demonstrator at King's, now back in the [[Strand, London|Strand]]. He remained at King's for the rest of his life. Milestones along the way were:

* 1946 — Assistant Lecturer
* 1947 — Lecturer
* 1956 — Reader in Physical Organic Chemistry
* 1964 — Professor of Chemistry
* 1971 — Head of Department
* 1975 — Fellowship of King's College
* 1978 — Dean of the Faculty of Natural Science<ref name= "frs"/><ref>'GOLD, Prof. Victor', Who Was Who, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 1920–2016</ref><ref name="Russell">Colin Archibald Russell and Gerrylynn K. Roberts (2005) [https://books.google.com/books?id=e_Mb-zRltjQC&dq=victor+gold+chemistry+Advances+in+Physical+Organic+Chemistry&pg=PA98 Chemical history: reviews of the recent literature], Royal Society of Chemistry, {{ISBN|0-85404-464-7}}, {{ISBN|978-0-85404-464-1}}</ref>

Gold's specialty was [[physical organic chemistry]]. His research focused on the [[chemical kinetics|kinetics]] of organic [[chemical reaction]]s.<ref name="Russell"/> He established the ''Advances in Physical Organic Chemistry'' publication series in 1963 and edited it for many years.<ref>''[https://books.google.com/books?id=IAeEmNwp4acC&q=%22victor+gold%22++Physical+Organic+Chemistry Advances in Physical Organic Chemistry]'', Google Books website</ref>

He initiated the development of the [[Compendium of Chemical Terminology|IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology]], which is published with a [[Gold (color)|gold-color]]ed cover and is known as the "Gold Book" in recognition of his work as its first author and compiler.<ref>[http://old.iupac.org/publications/compendium/ IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology], [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]]</ref><ref>[http://www.iupac.org/publications/ci/2006/2806/edit.html From the Editor], Chemistry International, Vol. 28 No. 6, November–December 2006</ref>

Gold was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1972.<ref name="frs"/>

Ten years after his appointment at King's, Gold married Jean Sandiford, who had read chemistry at King's. They had two children: Elizabeth Helen in 1957, and Martin in 1959. Victor Gold, whose home was in [[South Croydon]], died on 29 September 1985.

== Publication ==
*''pH Measurements: Their Theory and Practice'', Metheun & Co., London, 1956.<ref name="frs"/>
